links.note: 981 says that for those who know what is due (கடன் அறிந்து) and take on worth, every good thing is கடன்; Parimelazhagar glosses this as the good qualities being natural to them. 218 uses the same phrase, கடனறி காட்சியவர், for people who do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 218 shows one concrete case of 981's general claim: a duty that is felt as one's own does not wait on circumstances.

981 makes all good things the கடன் of those who take on சான்றாண்மை. 802 names one such item with the same words, சான்றோர் கடன்: being 'as salt' (உப்பாதல்) to the liberties a friend takes. The pair shows the general statement being filled in by a specific obligation in the domain of friendship.

982 says the worthy have only the goodness of character (குணநலம்), and that other goodness is not counted among goodnesses; Parimelazhagar takes பிறநலம் to be the goodness of the bodily limbs. 79 asks what all the outer limbs (புறத்துறுப்பு) can do for those who lack love, the inner limb (அகத்துறுப்பு). Both verses rank an inner quality over the body's outward parts, one for worth and one for love.

982 denies that any goodness other than character counts for the worthy. 407 says the handsome looks (எழில்நலம்) of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை). Both dismiss outward நலம் that has nothing inside it, though 407 measures by understanding and 982 by character.

983 lists five pillars that bear worth: அன்பு, நாண், ஒப்புரவு, கண்ணோட்டம், வாய்மை. 1013 singles out one of them: as all lives are fixed on the body (ஊனைக் குறித்த), சால்பு is fixed on the good called shame (நாண் என்னும் நன்மை குறித்தது). Read together, shame is one support among five in 983 and the seat of worth itself in 1013.

983 names நாண் and வாய்மை among the five supports of சால்பு. 952 says those of good birth do not slip in three things: ஒழுக்கம், வாய்மை and நாண். Two of the items recur, so the lists of what holds up worth and what marks good family overlap in truthfulness and shame.

983 calls its five qualities the pillar planted to bear worth (சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண்). 615 calls the man who wants the work and not pleasure a pillar that wipes away his kin's troubles and props them (துடைத்து ஊன்றும் தூண்). The same figure, with the same verb ஊன்று, is used once for qualities holding up a character and once for a person holding up a family.

984 says சால்பு lies in the goodness of not telling others' faults (பிறர் தீமை சொல்லா நலம்). 980, in the preceding chapter, says greatness covers another's weakness (அற்றம் மறைக்கும்) while smallness tells only faults (குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). The same test, what one does with another person's faults, is applied to பெருமை in one chapter and to சால்பு in the next.

The first half of 984 says austerity (நோன்மை) lies in the goodness of not killing. 261 defines the form of தவம் as bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்கு உறுகண் செய்யாமை). 984 takes over that definition from the Book of Virtue and sets not speaking of others' faults beside it as the matching mark of worth.

985 says the strength of those who accomplish is bowing (பணிதல்), and that this is the weapon by which the worthy turn foes. 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration. Both attach bowing to the strong and not the weak; 985 adds that it has an effect on opponents.

985 and 225 open with the same words, ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல். 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, and ranks it behind the strength of those who relieve hunger (மாற்றுவார்); 985 says it is bowing, the weapon that turns foes (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும்). In both the formula redefines strength as a kind of restraint, and both play on மாற்று.

985 presents bowing as the weapon (படை) with which the worthy change their opponents. 827 warns not to accept bowing in an enemy's words (சொல்வணக்கம் ஒன்னார்கண் கொள்ளற்க), because the bending of a bow means harm. Read from the receiving side, 827 limits 985: humility can disarm a foe, and a foe's humility can also be the drawn bow.

986 says the touchstone of worth is accepting defeat (தோல்வி கொளல்) even from those who are not one's equal. In 1327 the man says that in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்), as the reunion shows. Both treat yielding as the better outcome; 1327 is a lover's remark about a sulk, while 986 states a test of character.

986 asks what the கட்டளை of worth is; Parimelazhagar explains it as the touchstone for the gold of worth, and answers: accepting defeat from one's inferiors. 505 says a person's own deeds are the touchstone (கட்டளைக் கல்) of greatness and smallness alike. 505 gives the general rule of testing people by what they do, and 986 names the particular act that tests worth.

987 asks what worth has brought if one does not do what is sweet even to those who did one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்). 314 begins with the same words, இன்னா செய்தாரை, and says the way to punish them is to shame them by doing them good (நன்னயஞ் செய்து விடல்). 314 gives this as a rule of non-harming; 987 makes it the thing without which சால்பு has no use.

987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm. 998, in the next chapter, says failing in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness (நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்) is lowness (கடை). Both verses use the particle 'even to' (-க்கும்) to extend the virtue to hostile people, one for சால்பு and one for பண்பு.

988 says poverty is no disgrace (இன்மை இளிவன்று) to one who has the firmness called worth. 1044 says that even in the well-born, poverty (இன்மை) produces the slackness from which demeaning words arise (இளிவந்த சொல்). They conflict if 1044's 'even' is taken to reach people of character generally; if சால்பு is a firmness beyond good birth, 988 states the exception.

988 says want does not disgrace a person of firm worth. 657 says the extreme poverty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கழிநல்குரவு) ranks above wealth gained by taking on blame. Both refuse to measure the சான்றோர் by their means; 657 adds the comparison with ill-gotten gain.

988 calls சால்பு a firmness (திண்மை) that keeps poverty from being a disgrace. 1064 describes that firmness at work: the worth that will not consent to begging even when no means remain (இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு) is too large for all space to hold. 1064 shows what the poor but worthy person of 988 does and does not do.

989 says those called the ஆழி of worth will not shift (பெயரார்) even if the age shifts. 124 says the stature of one who is restrained and does not turn from his station (நிலையின் திரியாது) is greater than a mountain. Both praise immovability and measure it against the largest fixed things, the world-age in one and the mountain in the other.

989 speaks of the ஆழி of worth; Parimelazhagar takes worth as a sea and ஆழி as its shore, the people who hold firm when other seas leave their bounds at the end of an age. 8 calls God அறவாழி, which Parimelazhagar reads as a sea of virtue, and sets it against the other seas (பிறவாழி) that are hard to swim. The word ஆழி joined to a virtue appears in both, as the sea itself in 8 and, on Parimelazhagar's reading, as its boundary in 989.

990 says that if the worthy decline in worth, the great earth will not bear its load (இருநிலம் தாங்காது பொறை). 996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டு உண்டு உலகம்) and would otherwise enter the earth and perish. The two neighbouring chapters each end their argument with the same claim, that the world's continuance depends on a few people of character.

990 says the earth cannot carry its burden (பொறை) once the worthy lose their worth. 572 says those without kindly regard are, by merely existing, a burden to the earth (நிலக்குப் பொறை). The same figure is used from two sides: the worthy are what lets the earth carry its load, and people without கண்ணோட்டம் are dead weight on it.

991 says courtesy is easily reached by being accessible to everyone (யார்மாட்டும் எண்பதத்தால்). 386 says the land of a king who is easy to see (காட்சிக்கு எளியன்) and not harsh in speech is praised above others. Accessibility is a requirement of kingship in 386 and the entry to பண்புடைமை for anyone in 991.

991 and 548 share the word எண்பதம், easy access. In 548 a king who is not accessible (எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா) and does not examine and do justice falls and perishes by himself; in 991 being accessible to all makes courtesy easy to attain. The quality whose absence ruins a ruler is the one whose presence makes a person courteous.

992 and 681 share a line almost word for word: அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல். In 992 these two are the way called courtesy (பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு); in 681 they are, with qualities kings desire (வேந்தவாம் பண்புடைமை), the nature of an envoy. The envoy's qualifications are thus built from the same two sources 992 gives for courtesy in general.

992 pairs love with birth in a seasoned family as the two sources of courtesy. 958 says that if lack of affection (நாரின்மை) shows in a person of good standing, his lineage is doubted. Both tie affection to good family, so that in 958 its absence counts as evidence against the birth.

993 says likeness of limbs (உறுப்பொத்தல்) is not likeness among people; the likeness that counts is likeness of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1071 says the base look exactly like people (மக்களே போல்வர்), and that the speaker has seen no resemblance so close. 1071 is the ironic application of 993: the bodily likeness is complete, and it settles nothing.

993 denies that sharing limbs makes people alike. 704 says those who grasp what is meant without its being said and the rest are alike in limbs yet different (உறுப்போரனையரால் வேறு). Both use உறுப்பு for the likeness that does not count; the difference that does is character in 993 and perceptiveness in 704.

994 says the world honours the character (பண்பு) of those whose usefulness (பயன்) comes from doing good with fairness (நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த). 97 uses the same four words of speech: words that yield benefit (பயன்) and do not part from பண்பு produce நயன் and bring forth நன்றி. Parimelazhagar glosses நயன் as justice in both, so the cluster describes good speech in 97 and a good life in 994.

994 praises people of நயன் whose doing good makes them useful (பயனுடையார்). 216 says wealth falling to one who has நயன் (நயனுடையான்) is like a fruit-bearing tree (பயன்மரம்) ripening in the middle of the town. 216 supplies the picture for 994: the person of நயன் is of பயன் to everyone within reach.

995 says scorn hurts even in jest (நகையுள்ளும் இன்னாது இகழ்ச்சி), and that those who know how others feel keep courtesy even in enmity. 871 says enmity, a thing without பண்பு, should not be wanted even in jest (நகையேயும்). Both refuse the excuse of play for something hurtful, and both bring பகை and பண்பு together.

995 says courtesy is present even in enmity (பகையுள்ளும் பண்புள) in those who understand others. 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the person of courtesy who treats enmity as friendship (பகை நட்பாக் கொண்டொழுகும் பண்புடையாளன்). 874 takes the step beyond 995, from staying courteous toward an enemy to turning him into a friend; Parimelazhagar reads 874 as a matter of policy.

995 warns that இகழ்ச்சி, scorn, wounds even as a joke. 953 lists not scorning (இகழாமை) with a smile, giving and sweet words as the four marks of a true family. 953 names the trait as a mark of good birth, and 995 gives the reason for it.

996 says the world exists by resting on people of courtesy (பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டு உண்டு உலகம்). 874 says the world rests in the greatness of the பண்புடையாளன் who treats enmity as friendship (தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்று உலகு). Both make the world depend on the person of பண்பு, the general claim in 996 and a specific case in the chapter on enmity.

996 says the world continues because of people of courtesy, and would otherwise perish. 571 says this world exists because the great beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டு இவ்வுலகு). The two verses use the same construction, 'because of X the world is', for two closely related qualities.

997 says those without human courtesy (மக்கட்பண்பு) are like trees (மரம் போல்வர்), though sharp as a file. 600 says those without abundance of inner drive are trees, different only in having human form (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). The tree stands in both for a person who lacks the defining human quality, which is courtesy in one verse and drive in the other.

997 likens the clever but discourteous to trees. 576 says those who have eyes and do not extend kindly regard are like trees fixed in the soil (மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரத்தனையர்). In both the comparison is to something that has the equipment, a sharp mind or eyes, and does not respond to other people.

998 calls it lowness (கடை) to fail in courtesy even toward those who act without friendship or kindness. 579 calls it the highest thing (தலை) to extend kindly regard and bear with even those whose nature is to hurt (ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்). The verses mark the two ends of the same scale: good conduct toward the hostile is தலை, and its failure is கடை.

998 requires courtesy even toward those who do unfriendly, unkind things. 852 says that even if someone does what one cannot bear, intending division (பகல் கருதிப் பற்றா செயினும்), it is best not to do harm in return out of hostility. 852 gives the minimum, no retaliation, and 998 asks for more, that courtesy itself not lapse.

999 says that for those not able to laugh (நகல் வல்லர் அல்லார்) the great world lies in darkness even by day; Parimelazhagar takes நகல் as mixing with others and being glad at heart. 523 says the life of one who does not mingle freely (அளவளாவு இல்லாதான்) is like a tank filling without a bank. On Parimelazhagar's reading both describe the cost of not mixing with people, as lost wealth in 523 and a darkened world in 999.

999 says the world is dark at midday to those who cannot laugh. 304 asks whether there is any enemy other than anger, which kills both the smile and joy (நகையும் உவகையும் கொல்லும்). 304 names one thing that removes நகை, and 999 says what a life without it is like.

1000 says great wealth obtained by one without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று). 1008 says the wealth of a man nobody seeks out is a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of the village (நச்சு மரம் பழுத்தற்று). Both say a good thing is made useless or harmful by the character of its holder; Parimelazhagar reads 1000 as wealth that benefits no one.

1000 gives the bad case: wealth with a person without பண்பு is milk turned in a tainted vessel. 216 gives the good case: wealth falling to a person of நயன் is a fruit tree ripening in the middle of town. Together they show that the Kural judges wealth by who holds it, with a paired image for each outcome.

1000 uses a vessel (கலம்) whose fault spoils the milk poured into it, for wealth held by a person without courtesy. 660 uses an unfired clay pot (பசுமண் கலம்) that cannot hold the water poured in, for wealth made by deceit. Both figure wealth as a liquid and the fault as the container, the owner's character in 1000 and the means of earning in 660.
